text: The integration test `tests/test_opencode.py::TestRunResumeIntegration::test_resume_session_produces_contextual_reply` is flaky by nature — it asserts the LLM remembers a 'zorkmid-purple' secret across a resumed session. Real LLM behavior varies (refusals, paraphrasing) so the substring check ('zorkmid' or 'purple') sometimes misses. Re-running usually passes. If it becomes a CI problem, loosen the assertion to just check that msg2 is non-empty and contextually plausible, or replace the prompt with something the model is more reliably willing to echo back.

Symphony deliberately keeps the agent ignorant of Linear. The agent's final assistant message on a turn becomes a Linear comment; Linear comment replies are fed back as the agent's next user message. The agent has no Linear tool, no awareness of ticket state, no special prompt structure for asking questions. This 'dumb pipe' shape was chosen because (a) it kept the integration surface tiny and language/agent-agnostic, (b) it removed the need to design agent-side tool protocols for ask-human/post-comment, and (c) it made comment concatenation (when the user posts multiple replies between polls) trivial: just glue them with author/timestamp headers and feed as one user message. The cost is that the agent can't ever 'know' it's on Linear, which means it can't reference ticket metadata or other tickets unless we shove them into the prompt explicitly. If someone ever wants the agent to manipulate Linear state directly (e.g. close the ticket, attach a PR link), they would need to break this abstraction — adding an MCP/tool on the agent side and giving the daemon a delegation model. Don't add this casually.

We explicitly rejected the WORKFLOW.md-style configurable prompt template approach that the openai/symphony SPEC.md describes. The system prompt and ticket prompt format are hardcoded in the orchestrator. Reasoning: this tool is built for solo personal use with stable workflow needs; adding a YAML-front-matter + Liquid-template loader and a file watcher would have multiplied the complexity for no concrete benefit at MVP scope. If users start wanting per-repo prompt customization, the cleanest reintroduction is to look for a `.symphony/prompt.md` in the repo at bootstrap time and use it instead of the hardcoded one. Don't bring back hot-reload or front-matter unless there's a real second use case driving it.

QA-on-missing-workspace deliberately does not auto-reclone. When _reconcile_serve picks a winner whose workspace was deleted (typical cause: the ticket was previously moved out of an active state, which triggers cleanup), we comment+transition out of QA rather than running prepare() to clone fresh.

Reason: the agent never git-pushes (sandbox hides credentials by design — see AGENTS.md). The agent's commits therefore live ONLY in the local workspace clone. If we re-cloned for QA, _git_switch_branch would fall through to 'git switch -c' against the remote default branch, and .symphony/serve would silently run against base-branch code — i.e. QA would 'start' but serve the wrong thing. Refusing to start is the safer failure.

The supported flow is to QA *before* moving the ticket to Done. Done→QA isn't recoverable in the current architecture.

This would only become a sensible feature if push-from-agent becomes the norm (so the branch is reachable from the remote). The user has separately mentioned wanting Symphony to optionally not auto-create per-ticket branches (push target/creds/PR being out of Symphony's scope) — that change, if it lands, may revisit this decision.

We removed the `opencode.model` config option (was at `AppConfig.opencode.model`). The reasoning: OpenCode's own configuration already selects a model, and in the workflows people actually run — multi-step agentic loops, tool use, code edits — overriding the model from Symphony's outer layer doesn't add value. The option was effectively dead config surface.

Don't reintroduce a model selector at the Symphony level without a concrete use case. If model choice ever needs to vary per-ticket (e.g. cheap model for triage, strong model for implementation), the right place is OpenCode's config or a per-project setting, not a single global string in Symphony's config.

The removal was a breaking change (`feat!:`); existing configs with an `opencode:` section fail loudly at load via pydantic's `extra="forbid"`.

WebhookServer injects on_wake by creating a per-server _HandlerWithWake subclass with on_wake as a class attribute. Calling it via self._on_wake() binds 'self' as the first arg (because Python treats functions stored on a class as methods); to invoke the raw callable, use type(self)._on_wake() in BaseHTTPRequestHandler subclasses. This pattern is also used for _webhook_secret (set as a server instance attribute, accessed via self.server._webhook_secret in the handler). If the injection pattern is refactored, audit both call sites — the current shape is slightly unusual but minimal.

Daemon-posted comments are tagged with a visible Markdown footer of the form `*Symphony · {kind}*`, appended at the tracker-adapter layer (linear_tracker.py / github_tracker.py) from a `kind` string supplied by the caller (e.g. "workspace", "final", "error", "context: 37,074 tokens"). Detection uses the helper `is_bot_comment(body)` in tracker.py, which checks for the substring `*Symphony · ` (middle dot is U+00B7). This replaced the old HTML-comment sentinel (`<!-- symphony:bot -->`) because Linear's renderer does not strip HTML comments, making the previous sentinel visible and ugly in the UI.

Two alternatives were considered and rejected this round:

1. Invisible zero-width characters as a sentinel (ZWSP / ZWNJ, etc.). Rejected as hacky, fragile, and prone to leaking via copy/paste into human comments.

2. Filtering by token-owner user id via `viewer { id }`. Rejected because when running with a personal API token, this would silently drop comments typed by the same human whose token is used, causing the daemon to ignore genuine human input.

The marker approach also removes the need for a separate bot user identity (the previous current_user_id / bot_user_id / bot_user_email machinery was all dropped), letting users run the daemon with their own personal API token.

Setup-error retry loop fires off historical comments when last_seen_comment_id is None. _save_setup_error (and the ProjectConfigError branch of _resume_pipeline) used to persist last_seen_comment_id=None when the error comment couldn't be posted to the tracker. On the next poll tick, _has_new_human_comment(tid, None) returns all comments, so any historical human comment satisfied the 'new comment' gate and re-fired _new_ticket_pipeline every poll interval — symptoms: workspace metadata comment posted multiple times, 'New ticket pipeline starting' repeating every poll. Fix establishes a three-tier baseline hierarchy at both error-save sites: (1) error_comment.id if posted, (2) existing last_seen_comment_id if non-None, (3) most-recent comment id via Tracker.list_comments_since(tid, None) with a graceful None fallback on tracker failure. Whenever you add a new error path that sets setup_error or transitions to failed, preserve this invariant: last_seen_comment_id must never be None when comments exist on the ticket.

Ticket→session mapping (StateStore.sessions) is deliberately maintained lazily: snapshotted only at cleanup time and consulted only at _new_ticket_pipeline start, while TicketState remains the live copy of session_id/last_seen_comment_id. A full split (moving those fields out of TicketState into the sessions map) was considered and rejected — it touches ~a dozen call sites across resume/recover/failed paths plus a state.json migration, for identical observable behavior. Entries are durable (not deleted on rehydrate; only pruned when the ticket itself is deleted) so repeated done→back cycles stay correct. Also rejected: skipping cleanup for done tickets entirely — would cost one get_issue call per done ticket per tick plus unbounded disk until Linear auto-archive.

Timeout comments include the salvaged partial message UNTRUNCATED by explicit user decision (STA-79): the partial output is mostly tool-call titles, which _assemble_message already summarizes to one line each, so real-world size is modest. Don't add a truncation cap without revisiting that. Same session also chose to salvage the sessionID from partial stdout on first-turn timeout so retries resume instead of restarting — resume-after-SIGKILL was assumed OpenCode-safe (same as daemon crash mid-turn) but not empirically verified; if resumes after first-turn timeouts ever misbehave, the fallback is to null session_id in the initial-pipeline timeout handler again.

Observed in production (2026-07, STA-81 incident): any orchestrator failure path that posts a tracker comment WITHOUT changing the ticket's state self-amplifies — the posted comment fires a Linear webhook, which wakes the poll loop immediately, which retries the same failure and posts again, yielding a sub-second retry+comment-spam loop instead of one attempt per poll interval. The established pattern (used by _bail_qa_no_workspace and now the serve-start-failure path) is: transition the ticket state FIRST, and post the comment only if the transition succeeded — the state transition is the de-dup that breaks the loop. Any new failure path that comments on a ticket must follow this pattern.

Symphony refuses to delete a dirty workspace on the first cleanup and bounces the ticket back to Needs Input. The user accepted two costs explicitly when this was designed: (1) in no-push setups every ticket is dirty by definition (local-only commits are the only copy of the work), so closing any ticket takes two moves to Done - this is intended, it reads as a confirmation prompt; (2) orphan directories accumulate forever with no garbage collection, including full clones plus whatever .symphony/setup built. Ticket deletion is deliberately exempt from the guard: the user's reasoning is that deleting a ticket almost never happens by accident, while moving a ticket's state happens constantly. Rejected alternatives: auto-commit or auto-push before deleting (credentials are hidden in the sandbox by design), a config switch for a looser 'uncommitted files only' test, a force label, an expiry on the refusal, and simply keeping every dirty directory without ever bouncing the ticket (the user wanted the tracker-visible stop signal). If disk growth becomes a problem, GC is the thing to add - not a weaker dirtiness test.

The 2026-08 layout change (<root>/<id>/{repo,attachments,tmp}) shipped as a clean break with NO migration, per Stavros: he deletes all tickets before upgrading, so in-flight state doesn't matter. A migration was considered and rejected — partly because it would be mostly futile anyway: OpenCode namespaces sessions by project/worktree path, so moving the clone from <root>/<id> to <root>/<id>/repo breaks 'opencode run --session <id>' resume regardless; a migration could only clear session ids (fresh session, lost agent context), not preserve them. Keep this in mind for any future change that moves the repo path.

STA-115: the 'OpenCode freezes forever' reports were all one upstream bug — 'opencode run' answers permission.asked only for the top-level session (session-id filter before the auto-approve branch), so an ask from a task-tool subagent is never answered and the turn hangs. Three separate hangs were confirmed in the wild, all on external_directory asks from @developer/@code-reviewer subagents. Two facts that made this look infinite rather than slow: the production config (which lives outside the repo, in the workspace dir) sets turn_timeout_seconds to 18000, and a hung turn also holds one of the 5 pool workers for that whole time. Diagnosis technique worth reusing: ~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log is shared by all instances but every line carries run=<8 hex> and session ids, so you can locate exactly where a hung turn stopped; a hung run's only remaining activity is an hourly 'cleanup prune=7.days' line, whereas an actively working run (subagents included) never went quieter than 38s. Stavros will file the upstream bug; the fix on our side is deliberately server-side (OPENCODE_PERMISSION), not CLI-flag-side, because every --auto-style flag sits behind the same broken filter.

A daemon restart is the daemon's fault, not the human's, so restart recovery must re-run the interrupted turn by itself rather than ask the human to nudge the ticket. Two alternatives were rejected when this was decided: (a) keep the bounce to Needs Input and only fix the misleading comment wording, and (b) make the bounce truthful by advancing last_seen_comment_id so the ticket genuinely waits for a reply. Both were rejected because they make the human do work after every restart. The retry cap exists only to stop a turn that keeps dying from being replayed forever; it is not a general retry policy, and 'no auto-retry on failure' still holds for turns that actually complete and fail.

2026-08 (STA-127): a turn failed because the Anthropic API returned repeated 'AI_APICallError: Overloaded' for claude-opus-5; OpenCode retried ~6 times over 95s on its own, then exited 1. When this was raised, the user explicitly chose NOT to add a Symphony-side retry or backoff for transient provider errors, and instead to move failed tickets to the tracker's Needs Input state so a human reply drives the retry. The 'no auto-retry on failure' invariant therefore holds deliberately even for failures that are known to be transient — do not 'improve' it into an automatic retry without asking.

STA-156: tracker comments now post only the agent's closing reply, not the whole turn trace. Rejected alternatives, so nobody rebuilds them: (a) keeping the trace in a collapsible <details> block -- Linear does not render raw HTML, so it would show as literal markup (GitHub would work, but one behaviour for both backends was preferred); (b) 'answer first, trace below a rule/blockquote' -- keeps every comment long, which was the complaint. The accepted cost is that narration between tool calls is lost: if the agent explains something mid-turn and closes with 'Done.', only 'Done.' is posted. The chosen mitigation is prompt-side (a sentence in _build_initial_prompt telling the agent to put the whole answer in its final message), NOT re-adding the trace. The timeout path deliberately keeps the full trace (see wdfrgs).

Mid-turn comments are discarded rather than queued for the next turn, and the reason is the human's, not a technical one.

The obvious fix for a comment posted while a turn is running is to queue it and feed it to the next turn (make the end-of-turn last_seen_comment_id write land on the last comment the turn consumed instead of on the bot's own final comment; list_comments_since is positional, so everything after it replays). That was designed and costed at about 15 lines. It was rejected.

Stavros's reasoning: a mid-turn comment is written without having seen the agent's reply. Once the reply lands, the comment is often stale — he would have written something different. Replaying it makes the agent act on an instruction the human had already superseded. He would rather read the reply and copy-paste a fresh comment than have a possibly out-of-date one acted on automatically.

So the daemon posts 'I did not read this — I'm mid-turn' and drops the comment. Note README's Limitations section previously claimed mid-turn comments were queued and delivered next turn; that was never true, and the text was corrected rather than the behaviour.

A second alternative was rejected on scope, not merit: having each pipeline advance last_seen_comment_id at the moment it consumes its input. That removes the need for the in-memory _turn_input_marker map entirely (about four lines), but a daemon restart mid-turn would then stop replaying the triggering comment — _rerun_interrupted_turn would take its 'session id but nothing pending' branch and park the ticket with 'reply to continue'. That is arguably consistent with the same anti-stale-replay argument above, and may be worth revisiting, but it changes a documented recovery invariant and leaves part of the interrupted_turns machinery unused.

STA-169 added OMP as a second coding-agent CLI alongside OpenCode. Stavros chose to keep BOTH rather than replace OpenCode, explicitly because he wanted the abstraction (agent_runner.py + one adapter per CLI); replacing outright would have been noticeably less code and was the cheaper option on offer.

Three things were considered and rejected, so there is no code to comment on:
- Per-project and per-ticket ('Agent: omp' label, mirroring the existing 'Model:' labels) selection. Selection is global only, one config field, matching how the tracker backend is chosen.
- Profile isolation via 'omp --profile symphony'. It would isolate the daemon's sessions and caches from interactive OMP use, but also isolates auth, so it needs a separate login. Stavros said share the default profile for now.
- Relaxing the 'models:' alias validator to accept OMP's fuzzy model names ('opus'). Left alone: label values that miss the alias map already pass through verbatim, so 'Model: opus' works with no config entry, and only the alias map itself is restricted to provider/model.

Accepted unverified risk, agreed as ship-and-watch rather than build-for: five concurrent pool workers share one ~/.omp containing several SQLite WAL databases (agent.db, history.db, models.db) plus run/daemons. OpenCode has the same shape and works, but OMP leans on SQLite harder. Nothing was built to defend against it.

STA-200 added a per-project tier to the Model: label override (issue label > project label > agent default). Putting the per-project model default in .symphony/config.yaml was offered as the cheaper option and Stavros rejected it outright: that file is per-REPOSITORY, not per-Linear-project. One repo can be the target of several Linear projects, so a model default there would be a per-repo setting wearing the name 'project'. His words: 'this isn't per-repo, it's not suitable.'

Do not revisit this by adding a 'model:' key to ProjectConfig. If someone genuinely wants a per-repo model default later, it is a separate feature with a separate name, not this one. Note also that .symphony/config.yaml would need the model resolved after the clone; today _new_ticket_pipeline resolves the model before it resolves the repo URL.

Also considered and not built: reading a per-project default on the GitHub backend. This is not a design choice we can revisit — GitHub Projects v2 has no project labels at all (ProjectV2 has no labels field and does not implement Labelable), and GitHub issue labels are per-repository while a project spans repos. The only routes would be parsing ProjectV2.readme/shortDescription or a project-id-keyed map in daemon config; both were declined as out of scope.

Rejected: a user-specifiable agent launch command in config.

When adding the pi harness (Aug 2026) we designed, then dropped, an `agent.command` config key holding argv templates with {prompt}/{session}/{model}/{files} placeholders, so any pi-compatible harness could be added without code.

Dropped because the band it covers is nearly empty. pi and omp differ by ONE flag (--auto-approve vs --no-approve) plus the binary name; everything else (-p, --mode json, --session <id>, --model, @file attachments, trailing prompt positional) is already identical. A fork that keeps the JSON protocol will almost certainly keep those flags too, and a fork that CHANGES the protocol needs parser work that no launch command can supply. The real coupling is the JSON event schema, not the argv.

Costs that decided it: a placeholder mini-language, validation that can only check placeholder presence and never semantics, and a bad failure mode — omit --auto-approve on an omp-like fork and turns do not error, they hang until the idle watchdog kills them at turn_idle_timeout_seconds. That reads as a flaky agent, not a config mistake. Adding a harness in code is smaller than a user writing a correct template.

Revisit only if a third-party fork appears that we cannot just ship support for. The convergence the maintainer wants is already delivered by the shared parser (pi_protocol.py) plus agent_runner: with those shared, a new pi-family harness costs roughly ten lines of argv.

Maintainer intent: converge on fewer harnesses, not more.

Stated while adding pi (Aug 2026): the direction is "one harness for everything", not "more different harnesses". A separate backend per coding-agent fork is explicitly the thing to avoid, and a proposal that adds one should be pushed back on.

What this means in practice: the shared seams (pi_protocol.py for the NDJSON schema, agent_runner.py for sandbox/watchdog plumbing) are where new agent support belongs. Per-agent modules should shrink to argv construction. opencode.py is the standing exception — its event schema genuinely differs (top-level sessionID, tool_use trimming), so it cannot join the pi family without a real protocol shim.

Feature parity across harnesses is a requirement, not a nice-to-have: anything one harness supports (model override via Model: labels, attachments, context-token reporting, session resume) the others are expected to support too.

STA-220: linear.trigger_label became nullable. Stavros found adding the Agent label per ticket too much friction because every ticket in his workspace is meant for agents. With null, a ticket is triggered by active state (In Progress/Needs Input/QA) plus a Repo external link on its project. Two alternatives were considered and rejected: a new linear.team config field to scope the poll (extra config; Repo link already mandatory so it scopes for free), and flipping the default to no label (rejected to avoid surprising existing installs). Accepted consequence: in null mode any human-owned In Progress ticket in a repo-linked project gets picked up. GitHub trigger_field deliberately left as is.
